Sep 27, 2026 · ​@Master's Union
How this script works
The brand deck is an argument. It is split into sections, each built to persuade the room of
exactly one proposition, in a series of interlinked premises. The speaker's job in any
section is to land that one proposition and move on.
One thing per section. Every section has a single premise the room must believe by the
time you leave it.
Premises, not narration. Each section lists the premises that make its proposition true.
You say the premises out loud; the slides carry the evidence. Never read a slide, always
supplement
How to use it in the room. Read The case on one page to hold the whole argument in your
head. Read Audience routing to choose the route for who is in front of you. Read the
Section scripts for the sections on that route. Keep the Objection bank open on your
phone.
Four rules that never flex. The institution is always named in full, Masters' Union
University, and is never described as a business school or B-school. The average package
is never spoken without the median beside it. Memberships are never called
accreditations. Every claim you make must be checkable on a public page within ten
minutes, or you do not make it.
The case on one page
The 90-slide deck is seven sections, each carrying one proposition, in an order where each
proposition is the premise of the next.

How the argument runs. Sections 1 to 3 establish that the idea is right, and that it works.
Section 4 shows the machine. Sections 5 and 6 show what the machine produces and
where. Section 7 routes the listener to their own programme and asks for one thing. A
speaker who loses the room in Section 2 will not recover it in Section 5, however good the
placement numbers are: a sceptical audience has to accept the institution before it will
accept its outcomes.
Three lengths of the same case. Never shorten a section by talking faster. Shorten the
case by dropping whole sections, in this order.
Section 4 is the one section with sub-sections. 4A Learning Model (19 to 21), 4B Inclass
(22 to 28), 4C Outclass: Challenges and Competitions (29 to 36), 4D Outclass: Labs (37 to
42), 4E Funded Ventures (43 to 50), 4F Immersions (51 to 54). Each sub-section has its
own one thing and premises in the Section scripts, so routes can drop or keep them
individually.
Audience routing
The deck does not change by audience; the route through it does. Pick the row, run the
sections it leans on in deck order, and compress the rest to a single slide or drop them.
The opening line is the first thing said after hello. The ask is the last thing said, and there is
only ever one.

and it is being recognised for exactly the things it set out to do.

Slide 9, purpose. "Our purpose is one line: to build India's practitioner-led institution,
where students learn by building real products, companies and solutions. This is Learn by
Doing. And the vision behind it: to build a globally eminent institution that challenges
pedagogy and processes to deliver unparalleled human growth. Those are not decorative
sentences. You will see every part of them at work today: the practitioners, the building,
the challenging of how things are taught."
"First, what this institution is." LOCKED: "Masters' Union University. The bill has been
passed by the Government of Haryana." "That means a university's degrees and a
university's governance, built on six years of the model already running."
Slide 10, recognition. "The idea has been recognised beyond our walls, and I would ask you
to notice the pattern in what it is recognised for. Gold at the Education Excellence Awards
two years running, for a sustained, institution-led startup ecosystem with strong industry
linkage and founder outcomes. The Financial Express AIconic Award 2026 for the best use
of AI in education. Reimagine Education 2025 to 26, selected from more than 1,200 global
entries. A QS I-GAUGE Institution of Happiness certification for campus wellbeing and
student experience. The Indian Education Awards and the World Education Summit
Awards in 2026. Startups, AI, and how students actually live here. That is the model being
noticed, not the marketing."

needs people who have done the thing. Three leaders who built at scale looked at this idea

hundreds of millions and into Africa, chaired SoftBank's renewable energy business in

India and headed SoftBank India. He gave the first lecture on this campus in September
2020, to the founding cohort. Vivek Gambhir ran Godrej Consumer Products for seven

thousand crore as its CEO; he chairs boAt today and is a Venture Partner at Lightspeed.

built it to two million users; he now backs founders through Caret Capital and sits on the
board of the Government of India's Karmayogi Bharat. Between them: telecom, consumer,
technology, capital. Drawn from different disciplines, they lend the university wisdom,
balance and foresight, and they guide its long-term direction. When people who have built

managing a P&L and testing product-market fit against competition. Students here launch
and run successful businesses regardless of where they come from, and their success is

the proof that the model works and reliably produces results.
Premises.
1. Doing produces a kind of learning a classroom cannot: a P&L, a customer, a competitor,
a result.
2. The proof is people. Founders from the first cohort to the newest, undergraduate and
postgraduate, from every background.
3. It works at every age: joined at eighteen, founder at nineteen; joined at twenty-seven,
founder at twenty-nine.
4. It is public. Six student startups have pitched on Shark Tank India, and the founder sat
on the panel for a Campus Special.
5. Most students take what they built into a job, seventeen percent build, and the
Founder's Fellowship means nobody has to choose blind.
What to say.
Slide 12, the opener. "Why learn by doing? Because studying business in a closed, sterile
room is a fundamentally different thing from managing a P&L, pricing a product, or finding
out whether customers want what you made while a competitor sells next to you. You can
read about product-market fit. Or you can go and not have it for six weeks, and then find
it. The second one changes you. Let me show you what it produced."
Slides 13 to 16, the founders. Pick two or three of these for the room in front of you, and
say each figure exactly as the slide prints it, with its label. "Mohit Goswami, Mohit Paliwal
and Yugal Tamang came through our very first cohort in 2021 and built Eight, an Indian
audio streaming platform. It is loved by more than a million listeners, has eighty thousand
paying subscribers, and has raised ₹16.5 crore from Kae Capital and Venture Highway.
Vikas Kabra, also Cohort 2021, built Nivara, a lab-grown diamond jewellery brand: ₹15
crore in annual recurring revenue, three retail boutiques, a team of twenty-one.
Shouradeep Chakraborty and Upamanyu Chatterjee joined the postgraduate programme
at twenty-seven and built PlaySuper, a gaming commerce platform with sixteen studio
partnerships; it has raised ₹12.5 crore from 100X.VC and the IAN Fund, and they made the
Forbes Asia 30 Under 30 list while still in the programme. Raghava Kundrapu and
Akhileshwar Reddy are former ISRO scientists who worked on Chandrayaan, NavIC and
PSLV; here they built Sanyark, a deep-tech aerospace company, and raised ₹16.5 crore in
pre-seed funding. And it is not only the postgraduates. Arjun Goel is an undergraduate,
Cohort 2028. His company, Meta Fashion, sells clothing for Roblox avatars and the same
styles in real life; it has scaled to ninety thousand paying users through organic growth
alone and done ₹2.5 crore in revenue. Hritvik Arora, Cohort 2027, built Zenmo,
Brand Deck Master Script
Page 34 of 62

motorsport-inspired watches, ₹3.5 crore in gross revenue. Four students from Cohort
2024 built Lexi's, a gourmet sandwich cloud kitchen that was rated 4.5 on Swiggy and
Zomato within three months of launch and now runs past a crore in annual recurring
revenue. Different cohorts, different ages, different starting points. Same method."
Slide 17, the ages. "Notice the ages on this slide. Joined at eighteen, founder at nineteen.
Joined at twenty-four, founder at twenty-six. Joined at twenty-seven, founder at twenty-
nine. This works whether you come to us straight out of school or out of a decade of work.
The method does not care about your age. It cares whether you will build."
Slide 18, Shark Tank India. LOCKED: "Six student startups have pitched on Shark Tank
India, across Seasons 1 to 5." "Bullspree in Season 1, MemoTag in Season 3, Hive School and
Nexera Health in Season 4, Hookd and MetaFashion in Season 5. That is not a one-off. The
pipeline is built into the curriculum, and you will see the machine behind it in the next
section. This year Shark Tank India partnered with us for a Campus Special episode, with
our founder Pratham Mittal as a guest shark, spotlighting student-founded ventures from
across the country. Two deals closed on air, including ₹1 crore for Floreal, a crochet floral
gifting brand, and ₹10 lakh for Two Words Away, a private event planning platform."
Close. "Now the part I think is more impressive than any of that. Not every venture
works." LOCKED: "Some of those ventures failed. The founders came out sharper, and
most of them got hired." "Last year seventeen percent of the cohort chose to build. The
rest took what they had built into a job, and I will show you those jobs in a moment. And
for anyone who wants to keep building after graduation, the Founder's Fellowship pays
₹50,000 a month for twelve months, with a second shot at placements alongside the next
cohort if the venture does not work out. Nobody here has to choose between courage and
safety. The next section is how all of this actually happens, week by week."
For the room. School students want this whole section; ask them which of the four they
would have built, and use slide 17 to say eighteen is not too early. Parents get one founder
story, then the seventeen percent line and the Fellowship, so they hear a safety net rather
than a founder factory. Postgraduate aspirants and working professionals get slide 17 and
PlaySuper: twenty-seven-year-olds who switched. Recruiters get slide 18 and the bridge
to Section 5. Friendly press gets the whole thing; it is the story. Investors hear it as the
deal-flow preview, with the fund in 4E.
If they ask.

The one thing. You are taught by the people who run the companies, alongside serious
scholars and international faculty, and the mix is deliberate.
Premises.
Brand Deck Master Script
Page 36 of 62

1. The faculty is designed as thirty percent resident PhD scholars, thirty percent visiting
international faculty, forty percent practitioners.
2. The scholars own the curriculum and publish in the journals that shape business
research.
3. The international faculty teach full courses, not guest lectures.
4. The practitioners are named by what they run.
5. More than two hundred industry leaders, policy makers and creators have taught or
spoken on this campus, and Mentor Union puts five hundred more a message away.
What to say.
Slide 22, the mix. LOCKED: "Forty percent practitioners, thirty percent full-time PhD faculty, thirty percent visiting international faculty." "That mix is the whole idea in one slide. Scholars for why it works,
international faculty for how it is done elsewhere, practitioners for how it is done on
Monday morning."
Slide 23, the scholars. "Thirty percent are resident faculty: the academic backbone, PhD
scholars who build and anchor the curriculum and teach the fundamentals. Dr Bhupesh
Manoharan, our Director-Dean of Faculty, from IIM Calcutta. Dr Nandini Seth in
quantitative methods and decision sciences. Dr Garima Chaklader and Dr Muneer Kalliyil
in economics. Dr Aarti Sharma in finance. Dr Vipin Sreekumar in strategy. Dr Manu Prasad
and Dr Kashika Sud in organisational behaviour. Dr Ashish Bhandari and Dr Ajith Babu in
operations. PhDs from IIM Bangalore, Calcutta, Ahmedabad and Tiruchirappalli, publishing
in the journals that shape business research: more than fifty publications across FT50 and
A-star ranked outlets, on everything from how digital platforms shape responsible
consumption to gender diversity on Indian boards. This is the half that makes the degree a
degree."
Slide 24, the world's best minds, in your classroom. "Thirty percent are visiting
international faculty who teach full courses here. Professor Shad Morris from MIT Sloan
on strategy. Dr Benjamin Dunford from Purdue on management. Rachel Konrad from
Stanford GSB on communications. Dr Daniel Van Der Vliet from Cornell on family
business. Dr Garrick Hileman from Cambridge, Dr Zal Phiroz from Harvard, and colleagues
from NYU Shanghai, Seattle University and the University of Southern California. Full
courses. The phrase matters: guest lectures are what everyone else has."
Slide 25, the practitioners. "And forty percent are practitioners: founders, operators and
senior leaders who bring the real world into the room. Tanmay Bhat teaches how to get
viral and how to monetise as a creator. Arjun Vaidya teaches growing and scaling a D2C
business. Barkha Dutt teaches women's leadership. Thomas Kuruvilla teaches
Brand Deck Master Script
Page 37 of 62

management strategy. Nitin Gaur teaches blockchain, crypto and DeFi. Dr Avantika Tomar
teaches strategic HR. Vaibhav Jain teaches mergers and acquisitions. Malthi Satish
teaches community brands and marketing. Our Professors of Practice include a former
Managing Director of Morgan Stanley and a former Director of IIFL Securities. And
Edward Rogers, who was Chief Knowledge Officer at NASA, teaches the art of managing
complexity."
Slides 26 to 27, the room this campus has become. "Then there are the people who have
stood at the front of our auditorium. Policy makers: Nitin Gadkari, Kiren Rijiju, Amitabh
Kant, Rajesh Khullar, and Jagdeep Dhankhar, who as Vice President of India told our
graduating class, 'You are going to democratise the economic and business landscape of
the country by asking questions.' Entrepreneurs: Joe Foster, who co-founded Reebok;
Kunal Bahl of Snapdeal; Ghazal Alagh of Honasa; Nikunj Biyani of SuperYou; Karan Johar.
CXOs: Rohit Kapoor, CEO of Swiggy; Sushant Dash, CEO of Tata Starbucks; Bikram Bedi,
who runs Google Cloud in India; Vishal Dhupar of NVIDIA; Vikram Pawah of BMW.
Creators: Nuseir Yassin of Nas Daily, Raj Shamani, Sharan Hegde of The 1% Club, Chandan
Mendiratta of Zepto, on how to write scripts that get millions of views. More than two
hundred industry leaders. Our students are in rooms most people spend a career trying to
get into, and it is built into the syllabus."
Slide 28, beyond the room. "And when the class ends, Mentor Union begins: our on-
demand platform that gives every student access to more than five hundred mentors
across eighteen countries, from Google in India and Spain to BCG in the UAE and SAP in
Germany, for the questions a class cannot answer. What does a BCG partner actually look
for in a round-three interview? Is my idea venture-scale, or am I building a feature?
Somebody who knows is a message away."
Close. "Scholars, international faculty, practitioners, and two hundred leaders through the
door. That is In Class. Now the half where the money is real."
For the room. PhD candidates and academics: slow down on slide 23, these are their
colleagues, and the fifty-plus publications are the point; research support and teaching
load come from the Dean in writing. Practitioner candidates: slide 25 is the peer group,
and the peer group is the pitch. Executives: the people you would give up a Saturday for.

practitioners are the difference. Parents: the practitioner names are reassurance, the
thirty full-time PhDs are the academic seriousness. Say both.

real audiences, cook real food, manage a real fund and win real competitions.
Premises.
1. Dropshipping in Term 1: set up a store, build a product, price it, run the go-to-market,
get customers, compete at the Mela.
2. The Content Creator Challenge: learn marketing by becoming the medium.
4. The Masters' Union Investment Fund: five crore rupees of real capital, managed by
students.
5. Around them, one-day challenges on live briefs, Ground Zero, Elevator Pitch, Behind
Closed Doors and Off-Campus.
What to say.
Slide 29, the opener. "Out Class is the half of the week where the money is real. Let me
take you through a first year."
Slides 30 to 32, the Dropshipping Challenge. "It starts in Term 1 with the Dropshipping
Challenge. Every student sets up an online store, picks or builds a product, prices it,
creates content, runs ads, drives traffic, handles returns and customer service, and then
competes at our offline fair, the Dropshipping Mela, in Cyber City. It is a true first taste of
business, not a classroom project. Look at last Term 1. Ship Happens sold gifts and sippers
and did ₹37.8 lakh. OKAMI sold perfumes: ₹33.8 lakh. The Reel Store, electronics and
home appliances: ₹19.3 lakh. Team Jugnu, jewellery and utility tech: ₹16.5 lakh. The ten
teams on this slide did ₹1.46 crore between them, in one term, as first-year students.
Across cohorts, students end up doing between five and fifty lakh rupees in revenue in
their first semester. It changes them. Lifetime, the challenge has served more than 85,000
customers and generated more than ₹9.7 crore across 280-plus teams." LOCKED, the
audited cohort figure: "Fifty-five teams did two crore eleven lakh rupees of revenue at a
six point four four times return on ad spend, in the Cohort of 2026 challenge." "The first
lesson in business here is to build one."
Brand Deck Master Script
Page 39 of 62

Slides 33 to 34, the Content Creator Challenge. "The second challenge teaches
marketing by making you the medium. In the Content Creator Challenge students build
real audiences on YouTube and Instagram, mentored by people like Tanmay Bhat on how
to monetise and Sahiba Bali on what your first hundred days should look like. Four
hundred and fifty students have taken part, across 280-plus active channels, with 5.4
million cumulative followers and more than ₹25 lakh won in rewards and cash prizes.
Anurag Bansal has generated over fifty million views, is a LinkedIn Top Voice with 34,000
followers, and has worked with Zerodha, Razorpay and CRED. Madhav Nangru averages
1.5 million views on his conversations with founders and VCs, and runs a second account
with his grandmother that has 792,000 followers. Three undergraduates from the Class of
2027 built Cospire, a channel about unconventional careers: half a million views and ₹37
lakh in revenue from content. Sidhant Dhall hosted Incognito, a masquerade ball that drew
2,200 applications for 200 places. Siddhanth Vengali founded Angry Toast and drove ₹4
lakh of revenue through content. Tushar Chuttani signed a ten-month collaboration with
Mokobara worth ₹3 lakh. These are not hobbies. They are distribution, and our students
learn to own it."

Slide 36, the markets. "And then real money of a different kind. Students manage the
Masters' Union Investment Fund." LOCKED: "Students run a fund of five crore rupees
themselves." "They take real positions across equities, venture and startups, real estate,
commodities, REITs and alternative assets, with fund managers, portfolio strategists and
traders on call every month. In the period on the slide the fund beat the Nifty by 19.2
percent and the Sensex by 17.27 percent, and made more than five startup investments
alongside noted VCs and angel funds. Alumni of the fund are now at VC firms, hedge
funds and investment banks. They learn to think like investors, not students."
Around the challenges. "And in between, the sprints. One-day challenges on live briefs:
students analysed Axis Max Life's revenue data to test whether its app launch had a
measurable business impact; built a go-to-market plan for FamApp in a single day;
researched why premium consumers prefer imported spirits over Indian ones and how
Brand Deck Master Script
Page 40 of 62

Samsāra could reposition itself as a modern Indian luxury brand. Their thinking is
presented to faculty, practitioners and, in most cases, the companies themselves. Ground
Zero, our D2C case fest with SuperYou, drew more than a thousand registrations from
twenty-five institutions. Elevator Pitch: one minute, no preparation, then direct
questioning, because when an idea is stripped of presentation only the thinking remains.
Behind Closed Doors puts student founders in front of real VCs on camera, with InfoEdge
Ventures and Sauce.vc, and lets you watch what actually gets a cheque written. And Off-
Campus takes students into the headquarters of India's biggest startups, PhysicsWallah
among them, to decode the business maths on site."
Close. "By the time a recruiter meets these students, they have run a P&L, grown an
audience, run a kitchen and managed money. That is the difference between a case study
and a bank statement."
For the room. Recruiters: this is their section, a P&L before the interview, then straight to
Section 5. School students and undergraduate aspirants: this is the answer to what they
will do every day; tell it as a first-term story with a beginning and an end. Parents hear the
same story with the safety rail: capped stakes, mentors, and a showcase at the end of
every challenge; the exact challenge rules come from the Outclass team. PGP Bharat
aspirants: the store and the P&L are theirs too. Press and creators: students running
businesses on camera, and some failing on camera, is the format. Executives and
investors: one slide, then on.
If they ask.

register; team revenues, lifetime totals, creator figures, fund performance and the sprint

The one thing. The facilities are specific: machines, terminals and tools students use
every week, and software we built ourselves.
What to say.
Slides 37 to 39, the Makers' Lab. "Everything you have just heard needs rooms and
machines, and we built them. The Makers' Lab is where students build and test physical
products: 3D printers for rapid prototyping, so an idea becomes a model the same
afternoon; drones and drone systems; VR headsets for spatial simulation; and a Tesla Suit,
a full-body haptic and motion-capture system that is rarely accessible in any academic
Brand Deck Master Script
Page 41 of 62

setting in India. On the wall right now: a drone, a hexapod robot, a RaspRover AI robot, a
remote-control car, all built by students. Prototypes from this room go on to Kickstarter
and into the products students actually sell. Build, test, iterate."
Slides 40 to 41, the PwC Centre for Generative AI. "Next to it, the PwC Centre for
Generative AI, a working AI lab and experience centre built with PwC India at Cyber Park,
launching at Tower C. NVIDIA-powered data processing units, AI robotics and large-scale
data science systems, and students working on live industry use cases on them. It is built
to move AI education from theory to practice, which is the only kind of AI education worth
paying for."
Slide 42, the Bloomberg Lab. "And the Bloomberg Lab: Bloomberg Terminals available
around the clock, the same terminals a trading floor uses. Students map markets in real
time, link prices to news, fundamentals, flows and macro drivers, build a thesis, assess

The one thing. There is a machine behind the ventures: a structured path, a stage, capital
and a safety net, all named.
Premises.
1. The Venture Initiation Programme is a five-stage path from idea to Demo Day, over two
terms.
2. Demo Day puts founders in front of more than 150 investors, live, on YouTube.
3. Capital comes from three places: a student-run fund, MU Ventures, and equity-free
grants.
4. The Founder's Fellowship pays founders to keep building after graduation, and holds a
place at placements if they need it.
5. Named ventures with labelled figures, on every slide.
What to say.
Slides 43 to 44, the programme. "How early is too early to start building? Here the answer
is never. The Venture Initiation Programme is a structured, five-stage journey from idea to
venture, over two terms, with mentors, checkpoints and resources at every step. The Pre-
seed Challenge: identify a real problem and shape a solution, through expert-led
workshops and guided check-ins. The MVP Challenge: build and iterate a minimum viable
product and present it at the Annual Startup Fair, where the top ventures receive grants
of up to ₹30 lakh. The Go-to-Market Challenge: test channels, pricing and customer
acquisition in live markets. The Product-Market-Fit Challenge: validate with real
customers and get pitch-ready. And then Demo Day. Since 2021 there have been seven
editions, more than 185 startups built within the programme, 280-plus MVPs, and more
than ₹11 crore in equity-free grants awarded by the university. Some of the MVPs from the
last cohort: Unbrand, a lifestyle-first whey protein brand that did ₹5.5 lakh at MVP stage;
Stori.ai, an alternative credit-scoring engine; Oohlala, intimate wear for plus-size women,
thirty-two pre-orders in its first week."
Slides 45 to 48, the ventures. Pick two, and say each figure as printed, with its label. "Hive
School, a sales academy founded by Nikhil Gaur, Simar Sekhri and Prabal Monga from
Cohort 2024: ₹2.5 crore in annual recurring revenue, three cohorts trained, and its
graduates placed at a median of ₹14 lakh a year. Eat Atlas, gourmet dips and baked chips
rated 4.5 on Amazon, ₹80 lakh in annual recurring revenue. HOOKD, India's real chicken
chip, founded by Dia Goel, at a ₹1.82 crore annual run-rate and a Shark Tank India pitch
behind it. Cryptique, a Web3 analytics platform consulting in fifteen countries, ₹85 lakh in
consulting revenue. Guardex, an AI safety platform for factories, piloted across twelve
Brand Deck Master Script
Page 43 of 62

partner plants and incubated at IIT Kanpur. Yango, science-backed nutrition for kids, rated
five on Amazon, ₹27 lakh in annual recurring revenue. Khet, fragrances inspired by India,
₹60 lakh in gross revenue and ₹7 lakh in profit, from three students in Cohort 2027. Zhor,
a Gurugram run club five thousand runners strong, with Nike, Red Bull and Starbucks
among twenty brand collaborations. AceCard, an NFC business card, three thousand
cards sold. Every one of these has a website and an order button. Check them tonight."
Slide 49, Demo Day. "Demo Day is where everything built so far comes together. Selected
founders present market-tested ventures to more than 150 venture capitalists and angels,
with live audience voting, direct investor feedback and on-the-spot capital interest,
streamed live on YouTube. Vishesh Khurana, co-founder of Shiprocket, sat in that room at
Demo Day 2025. More than forty startups have crossed that stage. It is the moment a
student venture leaves campus and starts its life in the real world."
Slide 50, the capital. "Then the money, and there are three sources of it." LOCKED:
"Students run a fund of five crore rupees themselves." "MU Ventures is India's founder-
first early-stage fund for founders under twenty-five: idea-stage cheques of up to ₹10
lakh, hands-on mentorship from experienced founders and operators, and access to a
network of founders, mentors and investors." LOCKED: "MU Ventures runs a one hundred
crore rupee fund that backs founders under twenty-five." "And after graduation, the
Founder's Fellowship: ₹50,000 every month for twelve months, for every student founder
who wants it, with no cap on the number of fellowships in a cohort, and a second shot at
placements alongside the next cohort if the venture does not work out. Fifty-plus student
startups have come through the Fellowship, with more than ₹15 crore in grants and,
between them, more than ₹319 crore in annualised revenue. And the far end of the
pipeline is television: the six Shark Tank India pitches you saw earlier came out of this
machine."
Close. "A path, a stage, three kinds of capital and a safety net. Nobody here builds alone."
For the room. Investors and MU Ventures co-investors: this is their section; fund
structure, terms, deployment and the portfolio sheet come from MU Ventures, and the
named ventures are the deal-flow evidence. Government: enterprise and employment
created by people under twenty-five. Parents: the Fellowship's second shot at
placements is the sentence they remember. School students: the five crore student fund
and the ₹10 lakh idea-stage cheque. Press: named ventures with live websites.
If they ask.

Page 44 of 62

Numbers here: the five crore student fund and the hundred crore MU Ventures fund from
the locked register; programme totals, MVP examples, Demo Day, the Fellowship terms and
totals, and every venture figure from the 2026 prospectus, as printed.

The one thing. Students go and see how business is actually done, in India and abroad,
and they do it often.
Premises.
1. Some lessons only make sense when you experience the world first-hand.
2. Global immersions run one to four weeks at top universities, companies and factories
across Asia and Europe.
3. Domestic immersions run from Delhi to Bengaluru, from D2C brands to fintechs to
manufacturing clusters.
4. Bharat Immersions is a two-month add-on for our own students, and PGP Bharat is a
whole programme built on travelling to where business happens.
5. One hundred and fifty-two immersions were completed in 2025.
What to say.
Slide 51, the opener. "The third part of the week is leaving the building. Some lessons only
make sense when you experience the world first-hand, so we take students into real
markets, real cultures and real companies, where immersions, industry visits and field
projects show them how business and people operate beyond their current lens."
LOCKED: "One hundred and fifty-two immersions were completed in 2025."
Slide 52, global. "Global immersions run from one to four weeks at top universities,
companies and factories. In Japan: the Rakuten group, the Nissan plant at Tochigi, Daikin's
R&D centre in Osaka, the Kyoto Open Innovation Network, TeamLab Planets. In Singapore:
Temasek, Singtel, Agoda, Partners Group, ABC Impact. Across Europe: the UN
headquarters in Geneva, Station F in Paris, Électricité de France, the IESEG campus,
Philips Healthcare in Amsterdam, Rabobank, the Heineken Experience, the Porsche
Museum, the Mercedes-Benz truck factory in Stuttgart, Sanofi and IHH Healthcare.
Students sit with the Vice President of Temasek and the CEO of the World LPG
Association. They see how the world's best businesses are built from the inside out."
Slide 53, domestic and Bharat. "Domestic immersions run from Delhi to Bengaluru. A D2C
brand in Gurugram, a fintech in Mumbai, a manufacturing cluster in Jalandhar; the Farmley
factory in Noida, an ITC factory, Smartivity's manufacturing floor, Mundra Port, and the
Brand Deck Master Script
Page 45 of 62

Parliament of India. Students learn how Indian businesses scale, adapt and win, directly
from the ground. Bharat Immersions is a two-month add-on for our own students:
Lenskart's headquarters in Delhi, the Nivia factory in Jalandhar, the Eggoz factory in
Haryana, the Swades Foundation for rural development, Mundra Port. And PGP Bharat is
the programme built entirely around this idea: learn business by travelling across twenty-
plus cities of Bharat, forty-plus immersions in twenty-four weeks, from Adani Wilmar's
refinery to the airport cargo terminals where real business happens; with a six-week
Bharat Fellowship for eighteen to twenty-one year olds across ten-plus cities." Let the
PGP Bharat film run here if it is embedded.
Slide 54, the hosts. "Every immersion ends in a written brief-back to the host: what the
students saw, and what they would change. The hosts read them. That is why Payal
Polyplast, Samsara Spirits Lab and Eggoz invite us back, and why a hundred and fifty-two
of these happened last year alone."
Close the whole of Section 4. "Three parts to every week. Taught by people who run
companies. Practised on real money and real machines. Checked against real operations,
in Gurugram, Jalandhar, Mundra, Tokyo and Geneva. Now, what that produces."
For the room. PGP Bharat aspirants: this is their whole section; eligibility, cities and dates
come from the Bharat team. Family business promoters: factory floors are their world; talk
about what students noticed that the owner had stopped seeing. Immersion and factory
hosts: the brief-back is what they get, and a hiring pipeline that has already seen a shop
floor. Government: engagement with the real economy of the state, from Mundra to
Jalandhar. School students and parents: they will be on a factory floor early in the
programme.
If they ask.
Numbers here: the 152 immersions from the locked register; destinations, partners and the
PGP Bharat format from the 2026 prospectus.

The one thing. It is not all work; you will love your time here. There are fraternities to join,
sixteen clubs, sport, and a culture of competitions and festivals that students run
themselves.
Premises.
1. Always on, always building: that is life at the Union, and it is a lot more than work.
2. Home is a private room with everything in it, a lounge, a gym and a shuttle to campus.
Brand Deck Master Script
Page 49 of 62

3. Fraternities, sixteen clubs and student-run festivities give every batch a culture to
inherit and raise.
4. UnMUte and the High School Startup League bring thousands of students from across
India to this campus every year.
5. Convocations addressed by Nithin Kamath, Peyush Bansal, Sanjeev Bikhchandani, the
Vice President of India and Rohit Sharma.
What to say.
Slide 65, the opener. "Always on, always building. That is life at the Union. But it is a lot
more than work, and this is the part students remember longest."
Slides 66 to 67, home. "Start with where you live. The hostel is a home away from home.
Every student gets a private, well-appointed room with a study desk, an attached
washroom, air conditioning, high-speed Wi-Fi and a private kitchenette. There is a
recreation lounge with a pool table, foosball and board games, a fully equipped gym,
nutritious in-house meals prepared daily, an on-site café for late conversations,
housekeeping, and a two-way shuttle to campus. Friendships form in that lounge; more
than one company has too."
Slides 68 to 71, who you live with. "Then who you live with. Fraternities: communities
where students support, compete and grow together, inside and outside the classroom,
with traditions that each batch inherits and raises. Sixteen clubs spanning business and
creation, built over time and handed on. Student-led festivities that turn the campus into
a shared experience all year. Sport: at IIT Jodhpur's Varchas 2025, our athletes ran the
1,500 metres and the 800 metres final and competed in shot put and high jump. Our
postgraduates go on a leadership trek together every year. And more than once a year the
auditorium fills with students from across the country."
Slide 72, UnMUte. "UnMUte is our flagship cultural and business festival, and it is a proper
one: 9,631 registrations from students across India, more than ten competitions across
business, finance, music, dance and fashion, and a ₹3 lakh prize pool. Students, creators,
founders and future leaders come to compete, collaborate and show what they can do. If
you want to see this campus at full volume, come to UnMUte."
Slides 73 to 76, the city comes to campus. "The High School Startup League is our
flagship business plan competition for school students: inter-school and city rounds,
state-level selection, and a campus final where teenagers pitch to entrepreneurs for ₹50
lakh in grants, in front of Ashneer Grover, Ankur Warikoo, Techburner and Sarthak Ahuja.
More than five hundred schools, ten thousand applications, fifteen states. Our
convocations have been addressed by Nithin Kamath of Zerodha, Peyush Bansal of
Brand Deck Master Script
Page 50 of 62

Lenskart, Sanjeev Bikhchandani of Info Edge, Jagdeep Dhankhar as Vice President of
India, and this year Rohit Sharma, who told the graduating class that how you start does
not matter as much as how you finish. Harvard Business School students visit on their
India immersion to work with ours; Kellogg faculty and students have come two years
running to study how this model works. The world comes to Cyber Park to look."
Slides 77 to 80, the campus. Play the campus film here if it is embedded, and let it run. If
they are stills: "Classrooms with digital boards and full AV. The pitching zone, where ideas
get built, pitched and funded. The co-working zone, where students find their companies
and their co-founders. The auditorium, where they learn from CXOs and pitch to VCs. The
library. The cafeteria, where students build the next Starbucks. The Makers' Lab, the
Bloomberg Lab, the Food Lab, and a merch store that sells brands built by the students
who study here. Everything on this campus was designed around the same idea: give
them something real to work on, and somewhere they will want to be while they do it."
Close. "That is the building and the life inside it. Now, which door is yours."
For the room. School students and undergraduate aspirants: their section; let them ask
about the hostel, food, clubs and weekends, and answer from the slides. Parents: the
private room, the meals, the shuttle and the gym are the sentences they want; fees for
accommodation come from Admissions with the fee sheet. Government: a campus and a
festival that bring ten thousand students a year to Gurugram. Press and creators:
UnMUte, Demo Day and the High School Startup League are shoot-ready moments.
Faculty candidates and employees: this is half of why you would want to be here.
If they ask.

UnMUte, High School Startup League and convocation pages.

that door and what happens in its first term. "Which door is yours? Are you finishing
school, do you already have a degree, are you mid-career, are you running the family
business, or do you have weeks rather than years?"

leading firms across consulting, analytics, AI and product. The UG Programme in
Technology and Business Management, at the intersection of technology and business,
built around scaling organisations, launching startups and understanding how modern
companies operate. The UG Programme in Psychology and Marketing, blending
psychology, neuroscience and marketing to understand consumers and build brands. The
UG Programme in Data Science and AI, hands-on data engineering, machine learning and
applied AI projects. The UG Programme in Finance and Economics, with a specialised CA
and CFA pathway and real exposure to markets, valuation and investment decisions. And
the newest doors, Robotics and AI, where every project is benchmarked against robotics
research labs across the country, and Biotechnology, a lab-led programme built around
real healthcare and life-sciences problems."
"If you already have a degree: the PGP in Technology & Business Management, sixteen
months for experienced professionals, or the twenty-four-month Young Leaders Cohort
for fresh graduates. The PGP in Human Resources & Organisation Strategy, for modern
people strategy and organisational design. The PGP in Sports Management & Gaming, the
business of sports, esports, leagues and gaming. And the newest, Applied AI & Agentic
Systems, and Sustainability & Business Management."
"If you are mid-career: PGP Rise General Management, designed for working
professionals who want their next level, with classes taught by CXOs, MDs and founders.
The PGP in Capital Markets & Trading, with round-the-clock Bloomberg Terminal access
and twenty-plus asset classes. Strategic Business Management, twelve months of live
consulting challenges, go-to-market simulations and product-scaling projects. And the
Bloomberg Equity Research Programme, for finance professionals building institutional-
grade research skills."
Brand Deck Master Script
Page 52 of 62

"If you run the family business: Owners and Promoters Management, for owners and
promoters strengthening governance, scaling operations and preparing succession; and
the PGP In Entrepreneurship and Business Acceleration, for founders and business
owners who want structured growth and revenue acceleration. Both sit under our School
of Family Business, chaired by Rajiv Gupta, and both are applied to your own company
while you are still running it."
"If you have weeks rather than years: PGP Bharat, twenty-four weeks, forty-plus
immersions across twenty-plus cities, travel plus hybrid weekend classes, open to all
graduates. And the six-week Bharat Fellowship for eighteen to twenty-one year olds,
twenty-five immersions across ten-plus cities: travel, collaborate, build."
Slides 88 to 89, recognition. LOCKED: "Masters' Union University. The bill has been
passed by the Government of Haryana." "Members of EFMD, AACSB, BGA and BSIS, and
an NSDC training partner. Recognised across industry and academia: Gold at the
Education Excellence Awards two years running for our startup ecosystem; the Financial
Express AIconic Award 2026 for the best use of AI in education; Reimagine Education
2025 to 26, from more than 1,200 global entries; the QS I-GAUGE Institution of Happiness
certification; the Indian Education Awards and the World Education Summit Awards in
2026. KPMG is our academic partner for big data analytics, Grant Thornton for financial
markets and analysis. Kellogg and Harvard Business School send their students here to
study the model. And we use Dubai as a base to build global industry partnerships and
open international roles for our graduates." Read the awards exactly as the slide prints
them.
Slide 90, vision ahead and the ask. "Our vision is to build a globally eminent institution
that challenges pedagogy and processes to deliver unparalleled human growth. Six years
in: sixty students became two and a half thousand builders, a campus became a
university, and the departments coming next include law, medicine, agriculture and
biotechnology. Here is the one thing to do next." Then the ask for this room, from the
routing table: one action, one date, one link. The shape of every ask: "One thing to do
next: [the action], by [date], at [link]."
